theme: Taste and see that the LORD is good
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 34. David praises God for rescue and invites others to taste and see. Notice the movement from personal testimony to teaching, and the promises to the brokenhearted and the righteous.
settingTheScene: The heading says this is a psalm “of David, when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, so that he drove him out, and he went away.” It looks back on 1 Samuel 21:10-15, when David, fleeing Saul, went to the Philistine king and pretended to be insane to save his life. The psalm is an acrostic, each verse beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It is a thanksgiving for deliverance and a teaching psalm. Peter quotes it in his first letter (1 Peter 2:3 and 3:10-12), so it is a natural companion to our reading.
observation: “I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth” (v. 1).
“I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears” (v. 4).
“Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed” (v. 5).
“The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them” (v. 7).
“Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!” (v. 8).
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (v. 18).
“Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all” (v. 19).
“The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned” (v. 22).
interpretation:
David begins with a commitment: “I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth.” Not only when things go well, and not only when he is in the temple. This praise comes from a man who has just escaped by his wits and who admits that the credit belongs to the LORD. He invites others: “Oh, magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together!” Then his story: “I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears.” This poor man (the afflicted) cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles. “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.”

The center of the psalm is the invitation: “Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!” Faith is not only believing; it is experiencing. We do not just analyze whether a meal is good; we taste it. God invites us to try him and find that he is good. Peter picks up the image in 1 Peter 2:3, speaking of those who have “tasted that the Lord is good.” David notes that young lions suffer want and hunger, “but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.”

Then David moves into a teaching mode: “Come, O children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD.” The fear of the LORD includes keeping the tongue from evil, turning from evil and doing good, and seeking peace. “The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous and his ears toward their cry. The face of the LORD is against those who do evil.” Peter quotes these verses to encourage persecuted Christians that God sees their suffering.

The psalm’s most tender promise is verse 18: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.” God does not stand far off from the hurting. And it is honest about suffering: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken.” John quotes this verse in John 19:36, seeing it fulfilled in Jesus on the cross: not one of his bones was broken. The righteous sufferer ultimately is Christ. And the psalm ends with the promise to all who trust in him: “The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned.”
connection: 1 Samuel 21:10-15 is the background story. 1 Peter 2:3 and 3:10-12 quote and allude to this psalm. John 19:36 sees verse 20 fulfilled. Psalm 27:13 and 119:103 also speak of tasting God’s goodness. Isaiah 57:15 and 61:1 speak of the brokenhearted. Psalm 51:17 says God does not despise a broken heart. Luke 4:18 has Jesus bind up the brokenhearted. Romans 8:1 and 8:31-39 declare no condemnation. Matthew 4:11 and Hebrews 1:14 refer to angels serving. Romans 8:28 says God works for the good of those who love him.
application:
Practice taste and see: pause at one point today and thank God for something specific, noticing his goodness.

If you are brokenhearted, read verse 18 slowly and pray it as your own. If you know someone who is, sit with them.

Tell someone else about a time God delivered you, as David did in verses 1 to 6.
prayerPrompts: Bless the LORD at this moment, in your own words.
Thank him for delivering you from fears.
Ask him to help you taste and see his goodness.
